source_text: Θυσία δὲ ἡ τῷ θεῷ δεκτὴ σώματός τε καὶ τῶν τούτου παθῶν ἀμετανόητος χωρισμός. ἡ ἀληθὴς τῷ ὄντι θεοσέβεια αὕτη. καὶ μή τι εἰκότως μελέτη θανάτου διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται τῷ Σωκράτει ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὁ γὰρ μήτε τὴν ὄψιν παρατιθέμενος ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι μήτε τινὰ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων ἐφελκόμενος, ἀλλ’ αὐτῷ καθαρῷ τῷ νῷ τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐντυγχάνων τὴν ἀληθῆ φιλοσοφίαν μέτεισιν. τοῦτο ἄρα βούλεται καὶ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ ἡ τῆς πενταετίας σιωπή, ἣν τοῖς γνωρίμοις παρεγγυᾷ, ὡς δὴ ἀποστραφέντες τῶν αἰσθητῶν ψιλῷ τῷ νῷ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύοιεν. παρὰ Μωυσέως τοιαῦτα φιλοσοφήσαντες οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἄκροι. προστάσσει γὰρ τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα δείραντας εἰς μέλη διανεῖμαι, ἐπειδὴ γυμνὴν τῆς ὑλικῆς δορᾶς γενομένην τὴν γνωστικὴν ψυχὴν ἄνευ τῆς σωματικῆς φλυαρίας καὶ τῶν παθῶν πάντων, ὅσα περιποιοῦσιν αἱ κεναὶ καὶ ψευδεῖς ὑπολήψεις, ἀποδυσαμένην τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας, τῷ φωτὶ καθιερωθῆναι ἀνάγκη. οἱ δὲ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ θνητὸν ἐνδυόμενοι καθάπερ οἱ κοχλίαι καὶ περὶ τὰς αὑτῶν ἀκρασίας ὥσπερ οἱ ἐχῖνοι σφαιρηδὸν εἱλούμενοι περὶ τοῦ μακαρίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου θεοῦ τοιαῦτα οἷα καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν δοξάζουσιν. λέληθεν δ’ αὐτούς, κἂν πλησίον ἡμῶν τύχωσιν, ὡς μυρία ὅσα δεδώρηται ἡμῖν ὁ θεός, ὧν αὐτὸς ἀμέτοχος, γένεσιν μὲν ἀγένητος ὤν, τροφὴν δὲ ἀνενδεὴς ὤν, καὶ αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν, εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως ὑπάρχων. διὸ καὶ χεῖρας καὶ πόδας καὶ στόμα καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ εἰσόδους καὶ ἐξόδους καὶ ὀργὰς καὶ ἀπειλὰς μὴ πάθη θεοῦ τις ὑπολάβῃ παρὰ Ἑβραίοις λέγεσθαι, μηδαμῶς, ἀλληγορεῖσθαι δέ τινα ἐκ τούτων τῶν ὀνομάτων ὁσιώτερον, ἃ δὴ καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου κατὰ τὸν οἰκεῖον καιρὸν διασαφήσομεν.
pass_a_gloss: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the unregretted separation from the body and its passions. This is the true devotion to the existing God. And it is not without reason that the study of death is called philosophy by Socrates; for he, neither setting forth sight in his thinking nor being drawn to any of the other senses, but encountering things with the pure mind itself, pursues true philosophy. This, then, is what the five-year silence of Pythagoras wants, which he enjoins on those who know him, so that, having turned away from sensible things, they may contemplate the divine with the pure mind. The foremost Greeks, having philosophized in this way from Moses, command that the whole burnt offerings, having been flayed, be distributed into parts, since the gnostic soul, having become naked of the material skin and having stripped off the bodily chatter and all the passions, which the empty and false assumptions produce, and having put off the fleshly desires, must be consecrated to the light. But most people, putting on the mortal as the snails do and being rolled up around their own excesses like the hedgehogs, think such things about the blessed and immortal God as they also think about themselves. It has escaped their notice, even if they are near us, that the God who has given us countless things, of which He Himself is without share, being unborn, being without need of nourishment, and being in equality of growth, and having a good old age and a good death, being immortal and ageless, has done so. Therefore, no one should suppose that hands and feet and mouth and eyes and entrances and exits and organs and threats are passions of God, as is said among the Hebrews; rather, it is more pious to allegorize some of these names, which we will clarify as the discussion proceeds in its own time.

pass_b_english: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the unregretted separation from the body and its passions; this is true devotion to the living God. It is not without reason that Socrates called philosophy a practice of death: he neither brings sight into his thinking nor lets himself be drawn by any other sense, but meets reality with the pure mind alone, and so attains true philosophy. This is also what Pythagoras’ five-year silence aims at — he imposes it on his acquaintances so that, turning away from sensible things, they may contemplate the divine with the mind alone. The leading Greek thinkers, having philosophized in this way from Moses, command that whole burnt offerings be flayed and divided into parts; for the gnostic soul, stripped of its material covering and having put off bodily chatter, all the passions born of empty and false assumptions, and fleshly desires, must be consecrated to the light. Most people, however, clothe themselves in mortality like snails and curl up around their own excesses like hedgehogs, and they attribute to the blessed and immortal God the very qualities they find in themselves. They fail to see, even when they are near us, that God has given us countless gifts of which He Himself has no share: He is unborn, needs no nourishment, exists in equality of growth, enjoys a good old age and a good death, and is immortal and ageless. Therefore no one should suppose that hands, feet, mouth, eyes, entrances, exits, organs, or threats are passions of God, as the Hebrew scriptures speak of them; far from it. It is more pious to allegorize these names, and we will clarify them as the discussion proceeds in due course.

review.notes: Pass B fails to preserve the meaning of the Greek clause 'αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν' (growth in equality/proportion). Pass A translates it as 'being in equality of growth', which is a literal rendering of the Greek, but Pass B translates it as 'exists in equality of growth'. In the context of the Greek text describing God's attributes (unborn, without need of nourishment, etc.), 'αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν' refers to the concept of growth being in a state of equality/proportion/stability, or more likely, that He is 'being in equality [of state] regarding growth' (i.e., unchanging). However, Pass B's rendering 'exists in equality of growth' is semantically distinct from the Greek structure and the sense of the preceding attributes. More critically, Pass B omits the nuance of 'εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν' (good old age and a good death) by rendering it as 'enjoys a good old age and a good death', whereas the Greek 'εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως ὑπάρχων' is part of a list of attributes describing God's nature (being immortal and ageless). The most significant failure is in the clause 'αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν': Pass A's 'being in equality of growth' is a closer attempt at the Greek, but Pass B's 'exists in equality of growth' is a semantic shift. Furthermore, Pass B translates 'μήδαμῶς' (by no means/not at all) as 'far from it', which is acceptable, but it fails to capture the full weight of the negation in the preceding sentence regarding the Hebrew scriptures. Most importantly, Pass B's translation of 'εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν' as 'enjoys a good old age and a good death' contradicts the theological point that God is 'ἀγήρως' (ageless); one cannot 'enjoy a good old age' if one is ageless. The Greek is listing attributes that God *possesses* in a divine sense (or rather, the lack of them in a human sense) to contrast with human passions, but Pass B's phrasing creates a logical contradiction with the subsequent 'immortal and ageless'.
reasons: Pass B translates 'αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν' as 'exists in equality of growth', which deviates from the Greek structure and sense compared to Pass A's 'being in equality of growth'.

Pass B translates 'εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν' as 'enjoys a good old age and a good death', which creates a logical tension with the subsequent 'immortal and ageless' (ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως), whereas the Greek is a list of divine states/attributes.
